# Let It Crash: Large-Scale 3DGS Training with OOM as the Split Signal


---

## Abstract

Training 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) on large scenes exhausts GPU memory, and existing remedies all try to **prevent** the failure: heuristic pre-partitioning, Gaussian budget caps, out-of-core training. We take the opposite, pragmatic stance — **do not estimate or monitor VRAM; when OOM happens, use the crash itself as the split signal.** Training begins with the scene as a single tile. On OOM the failure is classified into four categories (immediate working-set overflow / allocator fragmentation / densification growth / inherited-payload overflow) and handled accordingly: fragmentation is retried in place, the rest split the tile and re-enqueue it. For growth-induced OOM, the trained Gaussians on every rank are emergency-saved at the moment of the crash through shared memory and POSIX signals, so that child tiles **inherit the parent's partial reconstruction (warm start)** — no training progress is discarded. Because splitting is reactive, no memory model, no profiling, and no per-scene tuning are required: the same command completes unattended on any GPU count or capacity, recursing only as deep as the hardware demands. We further show that geometric midpoint splitting produces systematic child imbalance (2.1–2.3× in our scenes) and that SfM point density is a poor predictor of final Gaussian density (r = 0.28), which rejects proxy-based balancing; cutting at the **median of the actually trained Gaussian distribution** instead reduces imbalance to ≤ 1.03×. On a 30-camera urban aerial scene (196 Mpx per image), two 24 GB GPUs completed a **71.5 M-Gaussian** reconstruction fully unattended over 2.8 days (16 growth-induced OOMs with zero data loss; one transient GPU loss recovered automatically). The merged scene matches an 8-GPU unconstrained single-tile run (oracle) in PSNR and **surpasses every baseline in SSIM and LPIPS** (35 % relative LPIPS improvement over 30 views; 84× the capacity — the oracle stalls at 0.86 M even when its densification threshold is resolution-corrected, because the same guard misreads pixel-borne pressure) — at a premium of 2.67× GPU-hours on hardware where single-tile training is impossible.

**Table 1 — The OOM taxonomy.** Classification requires nothing but the failure iteration and its position relative to the densification schedule.

| Category | Symptom | Cause | Response |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cat1 | OOM at iter ≈ 1 | Working set (images + SfM initialization) exceeds capacity | Split immediately; children start from scratch |
| Cat2 | Before densification, recurring at the same iteration | Allocator fragmentation (reserved ≫ allocated) | Bounded in-place retries, then split |
| Cat3 | After densification begins | Gaussian growth | Emergency save on all ranks → merge → split → **children warm-start** |
| Cat4 | Child OOMs at load time | The inherited payload alone exceeds capacity | Re-split while keeping the inheritance |


![fig](data:image/jpeg;base64,)
*Fig. 3 — Split progression (reconstructed from the §4.4 ours run; serpentine reading order). The background is the actual model state at each moment: from the initial tile through split 3 it is the SfM initialization (Cat1 splits carry no inheritance), and from split 4 onward the regions that inherited emergency-saved Gaussians grow visibly denser — warm start made visible. Red tiles are the two children created by that split (23 splits in total → 24 leaf tiles). The cuts sit at the measured Gaussian median, not at geometric midpoints.*


**Five claims, each with the section that tests it:**

1. **OOM-reactive tiling** — no VRAM estimation, monitoring, or offline profiling. The failure is the signal. (§3.2, §4.2)
2. **A taxonomy of failure** — not every OOM means "split": immediate overflow, fragmentation, and growth demand different responses. (§3.1)
3. **Crash-tolerant warm-start handoff** — trained Gaussians survive the crash and become the children's initialization. Nothing is retrained from scratch. (§3.3)
4. **Measured-median splitting** — balance by the trained Gaussian distribution, not by area and not by an SfM proxy; a clamp guarantees termination. (§3.4, §4.3)
5. **Unattended completion as a first-class goal** — the property practitioners actually want: run it once, on whatever GPUs exist, and get a scene. (§4.1)

**Positioning in one sentence.** Prior work spends its effort *predicting and avoiding* memory failure through modeling and monitoring — heuristic pre-partitioning [5–13], Gaussian budget caps [14, 15], out-of-core training via streaming or host offloading [16–18] (§2); we do only the arithmetic that is free before launch (image size, inherited count) and treat *reactively* only the one failure that is unpredictable in principle — OOM from densification growth, the growth that quality requires us to accept. Avoid the avoidable failures; use the unavoidable one as a signal.

**Contributions.** (i) Reactive recursive tiling that treats OOM as a **split signal** rather than an error, completing unattended on arbitrary GPU configurations without a memory model, profiling, or per-scene tuning (§3.2). (ii) A crash-tolerant warm-start handoff that preserves and inherits the training state of every rank at the instant of OOM, using only a pre-mapped shared-memory file and POSIX signals; the measured crash premium is ≤ 0.5 % of wall-clock (§3.3, §4.4). (iii) A four-way OOM taxonomy and measured-Gaussian median splitting, which empirically rejects the SfM-density proxy and reduces child imbalance to ≤ 1.03× (§3.1, §3.4). (iv) An empirical study: 71.5 M Gaussians completed unattended on a 30-view urban scene with 2 × 24 GB, outperforming an 8-GPU unconstrained run on SSIM and LPIPS (35 % relative), and a diagnosis of the "silent collapse" by which naive scaling loses its model before it dies (§4).

## 2. Related work

- **Pre-partitioned large-scale reconstruction.** Divide-and-conquer has been standard since the NeRF era (Block-NeRF [5], Mega-NeRF [6]). In 3DGS: VastGaussian [7], CityGaussian and V2 [8, 9], DOGS [10], Hierarchical-3DGS [11], HRGS [12], BlockGaussian [13]. All partition **before** training using camera poses, SfM density, or spatial heuristics, and all require block size to be tuned to the target GPU. BlockGaussian [13] is the closest to our work (content-aware balanced blocks) but estimates content by SfM point count — precisely the proxy we reject with measurements (§4.3).
- **Memory-bounded and out-of-core training.** Taming-3DGS budgets [14], Gaussians on a Diet [15], TideGS [16], CLM [17], A LoD of Gaussians [18]. These avoid OOM structurally, through caps, offloading, or streaming; they pay in throughput or in a ceiling on quality, and they still assume that the chosen budget is the right one.
- **Reactive memory management in ML systems.** DTR [19] discards and recomputes tensors on OOM, establishing the reactive-versus-planned distinction at the tensor level; cluster schedulers such as AntMan [20] and CARMA [21] restart or offload jobs that hit OOM. The underlying stance — do not prevent failure, make it safe — is Erlang's let-it-crash philosophy [22]. We carry that stance into **spatial decomposition of the problem with state inheritance**: rather than redoing the same computation, we permanently split the work and pass the partial result down.
- **Distributed 3DGS.** Grendel-GS [2] (the substrate for our per-tile training), RetinaGS [23], Splaxel [24]. These are orthogonal to us: they scale a single training run, whereas we schedule many.

## 3. Method

### 3.1 A taxonomy of OOM in 3DGS training

The taxonomy (Table 1) and its response paths (Fig. 2) were given in the introduction. The design point is that classification requires **no introspection of memory at all**: the failure iteration relative to the densification schedule, plus the presence or absence of an inherited PLY, separates the four cases (the classification step of Alg. 2). This simplicity is not accidental but structural — the four categories are overflows of four different resources (working set / allocator state / growth / inherited payload), and each resource reveals its limit at a different point in the training life cycle. §4.2 demonstrates each category empirically; §3.3 details the Cat3 path.

### 3.2 Reactive recursive tiling

![fig](data:image/jpeg;base64,)
*Fig. 4 — The recursive split tree produced by OOM (§4.4 ours run: 47 tiles, depth 8). Nodes are tiles; branches are OOM events.*


Tiles form a binary tree over the ground plane (X/Y). Each tile trains until convergence (best-plus-patience early stopping) or until OOM; on OOM its two children are enqueued. Termination is guaranteed by (a) the split-ratio clamp (§3.4) and (b) a minimum tile size. The scheduler keeps a persistent work queue (`adaptive_state.json`), so the entire pipeline is resumable after any interruption.

```
Algorithm 1 — Split-on-Failure scheduler (wrapper)
queue Q ← { whole scene = one tile };  persistent state adaptive_state.json
while Q ≠ ∅:
    t ← Q.pop()
    if level(t) < min_success_level − 1:            # preemptive split, from observed record
        (a,b) ← median_split(t);  Q.push(a,b);  continue
    rc ← torchrun(train, t, warm_start = t.inherited_ply)   # until convergence or crash
    if rc == completed:  mark t done;  min_success_level ← min(…)
    elif rc == 42:                                   # OOM split (Alg. 2 already executed)
        verify(sum of child rank-PLY counts == count at crash)
        (a,b) ← children from the cut coordinate in shared memory;  Q.push(a,b)
    elif rc == GPU lost: restart container, resume
    else:                re-enqueue (≤ 2×) or record failure
all tiles done → merge with bbox filtering → single scene PLY
```

### 3.3 Crash-tolerant warm-start handoff (Cat3)

![fig](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
*Fig. 5 — The Cat3 handoff sequence. At the moment of OOM the ranks may be blocked inside a collective, so coordination uses only shared memory and signals. The detecting rank computes and publishes the cut position, every rank filters against the same child bounding boxes, and the children read the per-rank files directly instead of merging them first.*




At the moment of OOM the ranks may be blocked inside a collective, so NCCL is unusable. The detecting rank writes the failure record (category, iteration, split coordinate; §3.4) into a pre-mapped shared-memory file and sends SIGUSR1 to its peers; each rank filters its own shard against the two child boxes and writes a per-rank PLY; the wrapper then verifies the counts per child. Children resume by re-sharding the inherited set into contiguous ranges.

**Anatomy of the OOM moment (hardware and OS level).** A CUDA out-of-memory condition does not kill the process — unlike the kernel OOM killer for host memory, a failing `cudaMalloc` surfaces through the PyTorch caching allocator as an ordinary **Python exception** (`torch.cuda.OutOfMemoryError`), leaving the process, the GPU context, and all existing tensors alive. Our system treats that property as a contract. The actual path from crash to verification:

1. **Catch and classify.** The exception handler in the training loop catches the OOM and classifies it from the iteration number and state alone: inside the first camera pass → Cat1; before densification starts → Cat2 (fragmentation); after densification → Cat3; immediately after loading an inherited PLY → Cat4. No memory instrumentation is involved.
2. **Compute and publish the cut.** The detecting rank computes the median cut coordinate from a sample of its local shard and writes the category, iteration, and coordinate into a 4 KB shared-memory file (`/tmp/oom_shm_*`) that was **mmapped at the start of training**. Pre-mapping is essential: in an OOM state a fresh allocation may fail again, so the coordination channel has to exist before the crash. If two ranks detect concurrently, the coordinate published first wins and the later rank discards its own — this closes the door on inconsistent child boxes across ranks (observed once, at split 1 of the §4.4 ours run).
3. **Notify.** NCCL cannot be used: peer ranks may be blocked inside a collective call, so collective communication would deadlock. Instead we send **`SIGUSR1`** directly, using the PID list exchanged by an all-gather at initialization. Receivers are covered twice: a Python signal handler (primary) and a 10 ms polling monitor thread (backup, in case the signal is lost).
4. **Free memory before saving.** Each rank releases its gradient tensors (`grad = None`), immediately reclaiming several GB. The monitor-thread path deliberately skips `cuda.synchronize()` and `empty_cache()` — synchronization right after an OOM is where we observed hangs.
5. **Filter and save.** Each rank filters its shard against the two child boxes and writes per-rank PLYs, watched by a timeout thread. While the saving flag is raised, torchrun's SIGTERM (propagated to the remaining ranks when one exits) cannot restart the save; it resumes from the point of interruption instead.
6. **Exit and verify.** The rank leaves via `os._exit(42)`: the standard exit path runs Python finalizers and tears down the CUDA context, either of which can hang in this state, and the exit code 42 tells the wrapper that this was a well-formed OOM split. The wrapper then checks that the Gaussian counts in the per-child rank-file headers sum to the count at the moment of the crash — a millisecond check that reads headers only, with no gigabyte-scale re-merge — and enqueues the child tiles.

Engineering that turned out to be necessary in practice, each traced back from an observed failure:

- **A save guard against termination signals.** When one rank exits, torchrun sends SIGTERM to the others; a naive handler restarted an in-progress save from the beginning, and on large tiles the restart exceeded the grace period and lost one rank file (observed once in 19 events). Raising a saving flag makes the handler stand aside, and the interrupted save resumes from where it stopped. Validated by signal-injection tests and then by three live firings with zero loss.
- **Fallback state recording on the save path** — a race in which the detecting rank's monitor thread outran the main thread's state write (≈ 100 % occurrence before the fix).
- **Concurrent-detection arbitration** — when two ranks detect OOM almost simultaneously, each tries to publish its own cut coordinate; keeping the first-published value prevents inconsistent child boxes (observed once).
- **Gating convergence decisions to intervals free of opacity resets**, otherwise a tile can be saved in the reset state and appear black.
- **Environment failures under the same philosophy.** We observed a container transiently losing its GPUs ("no GPUs found", a known consequence of host cgroup events) permanently failing a tile. Non-OOM failures are now re-enqueued twice, and if the GPUs are not visible at all the process exits with a distinct code so that the outer supervisor restarts the container and resumes. This is where the failure taxonomy extends beyond memory into the environment.

```
Algorithm 2 — Cat3 OOM handoff (inside a rank; pseudocode for the anatomy above)
try: training iteration
except OutOfMemoryError:
    cat ← classify(iteration, has_pretrained)        # 1/2/3/4
    if cat ∈ {1,2}: handle locally (retry / split signal), exit
    cut ← median(sample of local shard)              # Cat3
    shm.compare_and_publish(cat, iter, cut)          # first published cut wins
    for pid in rank_pids: kill(pid, SIGUSR1)
    raise saving flag;  grad ← None                  # skip sync / empty_cache
    for child in (A,B): my shard ∩ child.bbox → write PLY
    os._exit(42)
on SIGUSR1 (peer rank): read shm → run the same save with the same cut → exit(42)
```

### 3.4 Splitting at the measured Gaussian median

**One unified rule.** The splitting rule is literally single: *always cut at the median of the current Gaussian distribution (clamped at 0.65).* Only the source of that distribution differs by situation: Cat3 uses the trained Gaussians in memory (computed by the detecting rank and broadcast through shared memory, since ranks must agree on the boxes), Cat4 uses the inherited PLY on disk (computed by the wrapper), and Cat1/2 use the copy of the SfM initialization that happens to be in memory at the moment of OOM (a local shard suffices — no PLY is written, so cross-rank agreement is unnecessary). Because the initial distribution carries almost no information, its median simply lands near the midpoint (measured: the initial cut splits final mass 3/97, versus 4/96 for the midpoint — equivalent; the root cut sits at 47.5 % of the extent), and the same rule acquires information by itself as training proceeds. The geometric midpoint is not a rule but a safety fallback for when the computation fails. Informative pre-training estimates (pixel coverage, mini-probes) remain an open avenue for improving the earliest splits (§5).

Midpoint splitting is content-blind: in our scenes it consistently produces ≈ 32/68 child imbalance, and the dense child re-OOMs on load alone, cascading down to the minimum tile size until tiles are *skipped* — permanent holes in the final scene. Balancing requires knowing where the content is, and the SfM point count does not know: per-tile SfM counts correlate with final Gaussian counts at only r = 0.28, and SfM-sparse regions often end up denser, because densification compensates for the extractor's bias. The mechanism is straightforward. SfM points land where there is matchable texture (they are an artifact of the feature extractor), whereas Gaussians proliferate where rendering error remains — and every pixel must be explained regardless of texture, so a smooth untextured surface has few seeds but needs many Gaussians. Growth factors of 24–92× and the inverted compensation follow from this. The trained Gaussian distribution, by contrast, is not a proxy but the ground truth itself, and at the moment of a Cat3 OOM it is already resident in memory — it costs nothing beyond a read. At Cat1/2 the initial distribution is nearly uninformative, so its median falls close to the midpoint anyway (see the measurement above), and the imprecision of those first cuts is corrected downstream by the measured medians of subsequent Cat3 splits.

**Direct measurement of the proxy rejection.** Taking the final Gaussian distribution of a completed run (28.6 M) as ground truth, we retrospectively compare three candidate cuts at the initial split points:

| Parent (initial split) | Axis | Midpoint → mass ratio | SfM-median → mass ratio | Ideal (ground-truth median) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| root | X | 50/50 | 47/53 | 50/50 |
| tile_1 | Y | **4/96** | 3/97 | 50/50 |
| tile_2 | Y | **6/94** | 6/94 | 50/50 |

The SfM median is equivalent to the midpoint in every case — no improvement — reconfirming that the SfM distribution does not track final mass. The table also quantifies, honestly, the limitation of the initial midpoint split: in scenes whose content is concentrated on one side, a pre-training cut can be off by as much as 4/96, and the system pays for that with additional downstream splits driven by Cat3 medians. A third signal that estimates final mass before training (pixel coverage, mini-probes) remains an open direction (§5). **The cut rule**: split at the median along the longer axis, clamped so that the larger child never exceeds 65 % of the parent's extent (which guarantees termination). The detecting rank computes the position from a sample and broadcasts it over the same shared-memory channel, so all ranks filter against identical child boxes.

**Setup and implementation details.** A 30-camera urban aerial scene (Samseong-dong, Seoul; 11,310 × 17,310 = 196 Mpx per image; 579 K SfM points). Hardware: a node with 8 × Quadro RTX 6000 24 GB (2, 3, or 8 used per run) and 251 GB of host memory. Software: PyTorch 2.0 / CUDA 11.8, the Grendel-GS distributed backend [2] (bsz 1, pixel-partitioned rendering), in a version-pinned container. Key hyperparameters:

| Item | Value | Note |
|---|---|---|
| densify interval / threshold | 100 / 2e-4 | quality runs use vanilla defaults; only the OOM-stress ablation uses an aggressive schedule |
| schedule alignment | from / until / reset scaled proportionally to the iteration budget | reduces to vanilla at eff = 30 k (applied explicitly to the baseline as well in §4.5) |
| median clamp | 0.65 | termination guarantee (§3.4) |
| tile crop margin | 100 px | boundary context |
| convergence test | best + patience (min 1 k iters, 500-iter grace after resets) | gated to opacity-reset-free intervals (§3.3) |
| retries | 2 for non-OOM failures; container restart for infrastructure (GPU loss) | distinguished by exit code |

Run-to-run nondeterminism is stated in §5 (atomic accumulation, timing); code, configurations, and scene metadata will be released.

### 4.1 Unattended completion (system demonstration)

An early quality run (July 27) produced 37 tiles (19 leaves) with 13 Cat3 events, zero lost rank files, zero skipped tiles, and 66.1 M merged Gaussians in 2.5 days with no human intervention. A 3-GPU smoke test (odd world size) validated the full Cat3 cycle, including bit-exact merge verification across all 62 attributes. **Re-measured with the final code (the §4.4 ours run, 2 GPUs)**: 47 tiles (24 leaves; splits = 3 Cat1, 16 Cat3, 4 preemptive), 71.5 M merged Gaussians, and **every tile finished by convergence** — one mid-run container GPU loss was absorbed by automatic restart and resume, with zero human intervention (Figs. 8 and 9).

![fig](data:image/jpeg;base64,)
*Fig. 8 — Final tile map (§4.4 ours run — the same run as Figs. 2, 3, 5). 24 completed / 23 split. Colors encode the completion or split reason.*

![fig](data:image/jpeg;base64,)
*Fig. 9 — Per-tile final-epoch **training loss** (§4.4 ours run, 24 leaves, all converged). Best 0.0309 / worst 0.0855. This is a diagnostic of the end-of-training state, not merged-scene image quality — scene-level quality is the job of the PSNR numbers in §4.4. Red tiles are not failures but a reflection of content difficulty (the dense urban core, where all 30 cameras overlap).*

**The spread in per-tile loss (0.031–0.086) is not a defect of tiling but a structural property of per-tile training loss.** Three factors put the floor in a different place for each tile. (i) *View count*: tile loss correlates positively with the number of cameras (r = 0.49 over 24 leaves) — a 6-view tile fits its few views easily (and runs ~2,600 epochs, effectively approaching overfitting), whereas a 30-view urban tile must satisfy many viewpoints at once and therefore has an intrinsically higher multi-view floor. (ii) *Content density*: at equal view counts, the dense core (tile 0032: 12 views, 0.086) separates from the periphery (tile 1099: 12 views, 0.065). (iii) *Plateau-based stopping*: additional computation does not equalize floors. The spread is thus the kind that appears in any per-region training system, and it is distinct from tile-boundary distortion (§4.3b: boundary/interior scale ratio 0.94, 0.1 % discarded at merge). The fair arbiter of spatial quality is post-merge, scene-level error — and a direct cross-check that aggregates the 30 scored views of §4.4 over each tile's crop regions (Fig. 10) shows that **per-tile training loss and scene-level L1 are essentially uncorrelated (r = −0.05)**. The urban core has the worst training loss but the best scene-level score (0.031–0.039; the multi-view constraint of 30 overlapping cameras holds quality up), while the worst scene-level scores belong to edge tiles (0.058–0.070) where view coverage is sparse — a coverage effect present in any reconstruction, not an artifact of tile boundaries. In short, red in Fig. 9 does not mean "bad tile", and the training-loss heat map must be read as a difficulty diagnostic rather than a quality map.

![fig](data:image/jpeg;base64,)
*Fig. 10 — Left: per-tile training loss (Fig. 9 recolored). Right: per-tile post-merge scene L1 — one merged model renders the 30 views, the pixel error map is computed, and it is then cut by each tile's measured crop regions (from the training logs) and averaged. The two maps correlate at r = −0.05: training-loss spread is unrelated to scene-level quality, and the pattern of scene-level error is explained by scene-edge coverage. Two caveats about the aggregation: (i) crops include the 100 px margin and inter-tile overlap, so boundary pixels contribute partially to neighboring tiles as well (the effect on averages is negligible); (ii) "per tile" denotes region attribution rather than causation — it is the error over the image region that tile was responsible for, not the error produced by that tile's Gaussians, although in practice the two nearly coincide because out-of-box Gaussians are discarded at merge.*

### 4.2 The taxonomy, demonstrated

In stress runs, Cat1 appears at iteration 1 (the image working set), Cat2 recurs at a fixed iteration (fragmentation; retrying is only useful when it makes progress), and Cat3 appears after densification. Mitigating fragmentation (allocator GC threshold plus a max split size) extended root-tile survival from iteration 79 to 3,500.

### 4.3 Midpoint versus measured-median splitting (ablation)

Same scene, same seed, 3 GPUs, aggressive densification. **Child balance (five completed events per arm):**

| Cat3 event | Midpoint (area-based) | Median (count-based) |
|---|---|---|
| iter 153/237 (X) | 32.1 / 67.9 (2.12×) | 49.7 / 50.3 (1.013×) |
| iter 205 (X) | 30.6 / 69.4 (2.27×) | — |
| iter 268 (X) | 35.6 / 64.4 (1.81×) | 49.5 / 50.5 (1.021×) |
| iter 958 (Y) | 32.1 / 67.9 (2.12×) | 49.4 / 50.6 (1.025×) |
| iter 977/1007 (Y) | 31.5 / 68.5 (2.17×) | 49.8 / 50.2 (1.006×) |
| iter 1132 (Y) | — | 49.2 / 50.8 (1.033×) |

**Completion metrics (final code 4751d17; both arms completed without interruption, 2026-08-12/13):**

| | Area / midpoint | Count / median |
|---|---|---|
| total tiles | 19 | 23 |
| leaf tiles | 10 | 12 |
| max depth | 3 | 4 |
| skipped (holes) | 0 | 0 |
| uninterrupted wall-clock | **4 h 27 m** | 6 h 07 m |
| final Gaussians | 13.9 M | **33.8 M (2.4×)** |
| discard rate | 0.1 % | 0.1 % |
| median tile loss | 0.1172 | **0.0886** |
| Cat1 / 2 / 3 | 1 / 2 / 5 | 1 / 3 / 6 |

*(A caveat on depth: tile IDs follow the parent × 2 + 1 rule only for OOM splits, while preemptive splits use a sequential counter, so depth inferred from IDs is overestimated. The values above are recomputed from the actual parent–child relations in the logs; the 5/6 reported in an earlier draft was an ID-inference error.)*

**The key point: the two arms did not do the same work at different speeds — they did different amounts of work.** The median arm produced 2.4× more Gaussians on the same scene (33.8 M versus 13.9 M) and 24 % lower tile loss. The extra 1.6 hours is the price of that additional work; **per Gaussian, the median arm is 1.7× more efficient** (6.5 min/M versus 11.5 min/M). Balanced splits place both children in the memory headroom, so each tile trains longer and grows larger, whereas imbalanced splits let the larger child re-OOM early and cut its growth short — a direct consequence of the balance table above (2.1× versus 1.01×). Scene-level quality is settled by the table in §4.4: median 21.79 versus midpoint 21.11 dB, with SSIM and LPIPS also favoring the median arm.

**Effect of the optimization pass (2026-08-12).** Under identical conditions the area arm went from 9 h 05 m before optimization to **4 h 27 m after (−51 %)**. The contributions were a decode cache (re-decoding images per tile: 38 s → 10 s) and skipping the Cat3 merge (children read the rank PLYs directly, removing a gigabyte-scale round trip). Wall-clock decomposition after optimization (area arm): 81.1 % useful training / 11.7 % Cat3 recovery / 7.3 % Cat1–2 discard / 1.1 % cold start and save-merge / 1.8 % wrapper idle.

### 4.3b Blocking densification outside the tile box (ablation)

This is the treatment implied by the diagnosis of merge-time discards (the "shell" finding in §3.4), evaluated as an A/B under identical conditions (same box, same inheritance, and over complete runs):

| | mask OFF | mask ON |
|---|---|---|
| discard rate (whole run) | 4.7 % | **0.1 %** |
| total trained Gaussians | 41.1 M | **28.6 M (−30 %)** |
| tree structure | 23 tiles / depth 6 | 23 tiles / depth 6 (unchanged) |
| boundary distortion, same tile (boundary/interior scale ratio) | 0.94 | 0.94 (no distortion) |
| same-tile loss | 0.1300 | 0.1365 (Δ +0.005) |

Not growing a shell that will be discarded **completes the same scene with 30 % fewer Gaussians** — the compute and memory saved outweigh the discards avoided. The slight loss penalty is adjudicated by global quality in §4.4.

### 4.3c Evaluation protocol (the yardstick for §4.4)

Merged PLY → staged into a model folder → **half-resolution dataset** (8,655 × 5,655; at full resolution the 196 Mpx views push the rasterizer buffers to ≈ 11.6 GiB in dense views, exceeding 24 GB regardless of rank count — measured) → 4-GPU distributed rendering → PSNR/L1 over the 30 training views (**scene-level scoring**: one merged model measured against a single yardstick, not per-tile self-scoring; with only 30 cameras we do not hold views out — see §5). Applied identically to the oracle and to ours. Validation run: the mask-ON median scene (28.6 M) over 30/30 views, **mean PSNR 21.97 dB / L1 0.0462**.

### 4.4 Overhead against an unconstrained oracle

The ideal baseline for a memory-reactive method is training with *no memory constraint at all*. We construct that baseline explicitly: choose scene **A** so that original single-tile Grendel-GS completes on **C** GPUs (the oracle: time **D**, quality **Q**, count **E**) but does not fit on two, then run Split-on-Failure on two GPUs of the same machine — forcing it to tile — and measure the time to reach the same scene-level quality **Q**. The normalized overhead is

> **overhead = (T_ours × 2) / (D × C)** (a GPU-hours ratio; 1.0 would be ideal)

The arrival criterion is quality Q, not count E: tiled training has a different count trajectory anyway, because of boundary overlap and out-of-box discards. E is a secondary indicator.

1.0 is structurally unreachable — iterations lost before OOM, Cat1/2 restarts, warm-start re-convergence, and queue serialization are all pure cost. The claim of this section is therefore not zero overhead but **completion, at a measured premium, on hardware the oracle cannot use at all**. The decomposition of that premium (discarded iterations / restarts / re-convergence / scheduling gaps) is computed from the run logs and reported alongside.

One property worth stating explicitly: when a scene fits, Split-on-Failure never fires and the system is identical to the underlying Grendel-GS — **small scenes are free; large scenes pay the premium and complete unattended.**

**Oracle measurement (2026-08-12).** On the unmodified mini_30 scene with C = 8: **D = 6 h 20 m** (30 k iterations, no OOM), **E = 592,247** (+2 % over the 579 K SfM points), training loss 0.0969, **scene PSNR 22.87 dB** (same yardstick, §4.3c).

The count E revealed something: in whole-scene single-tile training, densification was effectively silent. The cause is that the vanilla 3DGS densification threshold is expressed in screen-relative (NDC) units, so the signal produced by a given pixel error scales inversely with image width — a one-pixel error in a 17,310 px-wide view is ≈ 1.2e-4, below the 2e-4 threshold — and in a 196 Mpx view most errors fall under the threshold. Tiling renormalizes that signal locally by shrinking the crop (the same error in a 2,428 px crop is ≈ 8.2e-4). In other words, **naive single-run scaling silently loses densification** — and yet the oracle still reached 22.87 dB with 592 K Gaussians, showing that a blurry but on-average respectable low-capacity reconstruction is possible. As a fairness check we re-ran the oracle with a resolution-corrected threshold (3e-5, a 7× relaxation; 2026-08-20): growth did start (579 K → 855 K, +48 %) but **the reserved-memory guard fired on all 8 ranks at exactly iteration 600**, and the remaining 29,400 iterations completed with zero growth (the checkpoints at iteration 7,000 and 30,000 contain identical counts). The oracle's low capacity is therefore not a threshold-setting problem but a structural consequence of the guard misreading pixel-borne reserved pressure (§4.5): **naive single-tile training cannot grow at this scale under any threshold.**

**Ours (completed 2026-08-15).** Two GPUs, quality settings (vanilla densification, 30 k iterations, no epoch cap), completed with one infrastructure retry. The tree has 47 tiles (23 splits, 24 leaves) and the merge holds **71.5 M Gaussians** (17 GB). **Measured T_ours = 67.6 h** wall-clock, including automatic infrastructure recovery (08-13 02:56 → 08-15 22:34). The normalized overhead is therefore **X = (67.6 × 2) / (6.33 × 8) = 135.3 / 50.7 GPU-hours = 2.67** — but since the oracle stalls at Q = 22.87 dB through densification silence while ours exceeds it (below), 2.67× is not the cost of reaching the same quality but a **conservative upper bound on the cost of reaching higher quality**. Wall-clock decomposition (`decompose_overhead`, the receipt): **76.0 % useful training / 23.9 % Cat3 recovery** (training up to the crash — not a total loss, since children inherit it) / 0.1 % Cat1–2 discard / 0.4 % cold start, save-merge, and wrapper idle combined.

**"Why not split before it blows up?" — the watermark dilemma.** The closest alternative is a proactive scheme that monitors a VRAM utilization threshold (a watermark) and splits just before OOM. Such a scheme cannot escape a dilemma in choosing that threshold. **(i) An aggressive threshold simply dies.** VRAM spikes are large, abrupt, and content-dependent — measured examples: a 1.10 GiB single allocation attempted with 1.0 GiB free (the death point of the 1/1 rung), a 9.01 GiB single allocation triggered by one particular view on a 24 GB card (§4.3c scoring render), and reserved memory reaching 90 % from pixel-borne buffers alone, with no relation to Gaussian count (§4.5 profile). Such spikes jump the threshold between monitoring intervals and produce the OOM anyway — and a watermark scheme, by construction, has no crash contingency, so **the entire training run fails**. **(ii) A conservative threshold cannot use the GPU.** To avoid dying, one must permanently reserve headroom equal to the largest spike — the measured 9 GiB spike is 38 % of the card, cutting steady-state capacity to roughly 60 % and making splits correspondingly more frequent. Capacity that cannot be used means more tiles, multiplied by the fixed cost per tile. Our design does not face the dilemma at all: **because crashing is safe (classification, lossless emergency save, inheritance), we push to the hardware's real limit.** The threshold is not predicted but discovered by collision, and the value discovered is by definition the exact limit for that GPU, that content, and that moment — the crash-safety machinery is not a post-hoc cost but **the key that unlocks full VRAM utilization.**

What remains is the price of that machinery, and the decomposition above answers it: the 23.9 % spent on Cat3 recovery is training time on the parent tile that a perfect proactive scheme would spend identically up to the split (and both approaches need the same save/split/inherit machinery), so the cost incurred purely *because* we crash is 0.4 % (cold start, save-merge, idle) + 0.1 % (Cat1/2 discards) = **≈ 0.5 % of wall-clock**. Even a perfect threshold obtained for free could therefore save at most 0.5 %, while the cost of a wrong threshold is unbounded, per the dilemma above. Fragmentation OOM (Cat2) fires with headroom to spare, so a crash path is needed even if one chooses the proactive route. Our own preemptive splitting is not an exception to this principle but an extension of it: it fires only on an **observed record** (skip the attempt when a tile is two or more levels larger than the smallest level a sibling has successfully completed), never on a predicted threshold.

**Final image-quality scoring (the §4.3c yardstick, all 30 views; 2026-08-18 to 20).**

| | Gaussians | GPUs | PSNR↑ | SSIM↑ | LPIPS↓ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **ours** | 71.5 M | 2 | 23.28 ± 0.32 | **0.750 ± 0.021** | **0.272 ± 0.029** |
| oracle, original (thr 2e-4) | 0.59 M | 8 | 22.87 ± 0.48 | 0.667 ± 0.020 | 0.466 ± 0.030 |
| oracle, corrected (thr 3e-5) | 0.86 M | 8 | **23.61 ± 0.48** | 0.704 ± 0.020 | 0.417 ± 0.030 |
| median arm | 33.8 M | 3 | 21.79 ± 0.74 | 0.662 ± 0.049 | 0.443 ± 0.070 |
| midpoint arm | 13.9 M | 3 | 21.11 ± 0.93 | 0.608 ± 0.063 | 0.518 ± 0.080 |

*(mean ± std over 30 views, half-resolution scene-level scoring; SSIM from scikit-image, LPIPS with AlexNet averaged over 4 × 4 tiles.)*

We record this honestly: **on PSNR alone the corrected oracle is the best.** Yet on the same 30 views **ours leads every model on SSIM and LPIPS** — LPIPS 0.272 versus 0.417 for the corrected oracle, a 35 % relative gap. This is not a reversal of quality but a **bias in PSNR**: half-resolution PSNR is forgiving of blur, because downsampling erases the high frequencies, whereas structural (SSIM) and perceptual (LPIPS) metrics see the detail that capacity buys. Comparing full-resolution detail crops of the same area directly against ground truth (Fig. 17) makes this concrete: PSNR is a tie (23.15 versus 23.04 — PSNR does not reward sharpness even at full resolution), but **SSIM 0.723 versus 0.697 and LPIPS 0.360 versus 0.466 (23 % better perceptual quality)** separate the two, and visually ours preserves crosswalks, road markings, and building outlines while the 855 K oracle smears roads and shows pronounced splat bleeding (the 10 cm-GSD orthophoto of Fig. 13 is simply not a product 855 K Gaussians can support). In summary: **PSNR is a yardstick blind to an 84× capacity gap; the value of capacity shows up in perceptual metrics and in downstream products.** Three measurement-reliability incidents and their fixes (host-RAM float64 expansion → fp32 loader with immediate release / GPU fragmentation → max_split_size / another user occupying GPUs → rank re-placement) are folded into the §4.3c protocol, whose completion test is now the **number of scored views (n = 30)** rather than the existence of an output file.

### 4.5 The staircase sweep — where the cliff is, and the silent collapse before it

On the same two GPUs (24 GB × 2) we raise scene resolution through 1/4 → 1/2 → 1/1 and run original (single-tile Grendel-GS) and ours side by side for 10 k iterations. The goal is not final quality but **where original dies, and what it loses before dying**.

**First sweep (2026-08-17): completion status and model state.**

| Rung | original | ours |
|---|---|---|
| 1/4 | completed, 16.3 M | completed, 6.8 M (no split fired) |
| 1/2 | completed, but **densification permanently stopped at iter 601**, ending at 0.61 M | completed, 6.7 M (no split fired) |
| 1/1 | **OOM after 2 m 10 s, before finishing even iteration 1** (SSIM conv2d fails a 1.10 GiB allocation, both ranks simultaneously) — no output at all | **completed in 15 h 25 m**, 25 tiles (12 splits), 18.3 M |

Two findings. First, the cliff (1/1) is unambiguous: original dies right after loading the initial points, while ours completes on the same hardware. Second, and more interesting, is the **silent collapse before the cliff**: at 1/2, original printed "Reserved memory … stop densification", permanently abandoned growth, and finished with 0.61 M — one twenty-seventh of the 16.3 M it produced at 1/4. Together with the oracle's densification silence in §4.4, this shows that naive scaling **loses the model beneath the appearance of completion** before it ever dies.

**The first sweep's timing comparison was invalid — schedule mismatch.** Our wrapper scales the densification and opacity schedules in proportion to the iteration budget (10 k), while original kept its 30 k-based constants (densify 500–15,000 versus 167–5,000; opacity reset 3,000 versus 1,000; LR decay over 30 k versus 10 k). The 25 % speed advantage ours showed at 1/4 was not overhead but a growth window half as long — the 16.3 M versus 6.8 M counts are the evidence. **Second sweep (2026-08-18), with schedules aligned**: original was given the identical densification schedule and a single save, and 1/4 and 1/2 were re-run:

| Rung | original | ours | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1/4 (n = 3 repeats) | 36 m 01 s ± 10 s, 6.838 M ± 0.023 M | 34 m 31 s ± 23 s, 6.808 M ± 0.005 M | **Overhead ≈ 0 under equal work** (0.4 % difference in counts between arms) — the ratio is 0.959 ± 0.006, i.e. ours is 4.1 % ± 0.6 % faster, a small systematic edge we attribute to loader and preprocessing paths; the cost of the OOM machinery is below the detection floor |
| 1/2 | 1 h 47 m 45 s, **0.58 M — the guard fires at the very first densification attempt (iter 200); growth never happens (0.58 M = the SfM initialization itself)** | 1 h 36 m 42 s, 6.73 M | The silent collapse reproduces after alignment, and earlier; with an 11.5× difference in model size, the timing comparison is meaningless |

The 1/1 rung needed no re-run (death precedes any schedule effect, so the first-sweep result stands).

**Profiling the 1/2 rung (2026-08-19, from logs).** Three things are established. (i) **What the collapse actually is**: in the aligned run, original's densification guard (reserved ≥ 90 %) fired at the **very first densification attempt (iteration 200)** — the final 0.58 M is not growth that stopped but growth that **never happened**, leaving the SfM initialization (579 K) essentially untouched. (ii) **What the guard misreads**: at that moment both arms held effectively the same number of Gaussians (≈ 0.58 M), so what filled the reserved pool was not Gaussians but **transient buffers created by image size** — the legacy SSIM convolution chain over a 3 × 4,384 × 5,655 loss strip per rank (the very function that produced the OOM at the 1/1 rung), plus a 4.4 GB dataset preloaded to the GPU. A reserved-based capacity guard misreads pixel-borne cache pressure as "Gaussian capacity exhausted" — this is the mechanism of the silent collapse. (iii) **The structure of the speed gap** (per-iteration measurements): over the identical-model interval (iter < 601), ours runs at 2.74 versus original's 1.75 it/s — 36 % slower for the same work; and even at the end (ours 6.7 M versus original 0.58 M, an 11.5× difference) the rates are 1.56 versus 1.82 it/s, only 14 % apart. At this resolution iteration cost is pixel-dominated (11.5× the Gaussians costs +17 % time), and what separated the wall-clock was not model size but the uniform tax of allocator pressure at the reserved ceiling. Exactly where ours keeps reserved memory below that ceiling, given the same guard and the same loss code, is not yet established **[TODO — re-run with memory_reserved instrumentation]**; fused SSIM was unavailable and fell back on both arms, so it is not a variable.

- Cat2 retry policy (recurrence at the same iteration ⇒ split early) — data collected, policy undecided.
- Generality across GPU budgets: {2, 3} × 24 GB done; smaller VRAM and larger GPU counts **[TODO]**.
- Standard benchmarks (Mill-19 / MatrixCity) with quantitative comparison against VastGaussian / CityGaussian / BlockGaussian **[TODO]**.

## 5. Limitations

- Box inheritance discards Gaussians that drift outside the parent box (0.65 % early, rising to 5.3 % late in a stress run); the visual cost is not quantified.
- Reactive splitting spends the iterations that precede the failure; we do not claim time-optimality against a *perfectly tuned* pre-partition — the claim is completion without tuning.
- The evaluation is currently a single scene family; the generality argument rests on the taxonomy and is not yet supported by breadth.
- **We do not claim run-to-run reproducibility (determinism).** Atomic accumulation in the rasterizer backward pass changes summation order between runs, producing small numerical differences; Gaussians sitting near the densification threshold flip between growing and not growing, and the difference accumulates over iterations — so repeated runs of the same configuration differ slightly in final count and split tree (measured over three repeats of the 1/4 rung: run-to-run count variation ±0.33 % for original and ±0.07 % for ours, with a 0.4 % difference between arms; §4.5). Nondeterminism is accepted here as in standard 3DGS practice. OOM itself is likewise a physical event that depends on allocator state and kernel timing. What this system guarantees is **not reproduction of a tree but completion on whatever tree arises.**
- Scoring is post-merge and scene-level, but over the 30 training views: with only 30 cameras we did not hold views out (all baselines are scored identically, so relative comparison remains valid; camera hold-out is planned for the standard benchmarks).

## 6. Conclusion

For the memory problem in large-scale 3DGS training, this paper designs for **recovery** rather than prevention. If OOM is treated as a classifiable signal, and the training state at the moment of the crash is inherited losslessly using only OS primitives (a pre-mapped shared-memory file and POSIX signals), the system finds its own splitting depth at the hardware's real limit — with no memory model and no threshold. The measured price is 0.5 % of wall-clock (the crash premium), and what it buys is a property watermark-based schemes structurally cannot have: **full VRAM utilization together with a guarantee of unattended completion**. On the same hardware, naive single-tile training either died (1/1) or collapsed silently before dying (growth halted at 0.58–0.86 M), and we traced that behavior to a predictive guard that misreads pixel-borne memory pressure as Gaussian capacity. Completing a 71.5 M-Gaussian scene on two 24 GB GPUs over three days without human intervention — and extracting a 10 cm-GSD orthophoto from it — demonstrates the practicality of the design.

**Future work.** Quantitative comparison against prior methods on standard benchmarks (Mill-19 / MatrixCity); extension to heterogeneous GPU pools and multiple nodes; informative pre-training signals for the earliest splits (pixel coverage, mini-probes); and a precise profile of allocator pressure based on reserved-memory instrumentation.
